summary: This paper investigates the impact of natural, functionality-preserving code transformations mined from real-world commits on the performance of AI agents performing vulnerability analysis. The authors find that applying these transformations significantly reduces the success rates of frontier agents (such as GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex) from 63.3% to 36.8%, and composing multiple transformations reduces it further to 20.0%. The study demonstrates that natural code transformations can serve as an effective defense to protect source code against malicious agentic scanning.

chk_problem.paper_excerpt:
arXiv:2610.14350v1 [cs.CR] 9 Oct 2026

A BSTRACT
Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI
agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today’s software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks,
giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line,
our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding:
agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that
carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears
consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations
derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense
against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining
recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to
evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively “confuse” frontier agents, e.g., Codex
with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger
protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of
natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code
transformations to defend against malicious agents.

1

I NTRODUCTION

Frontier AI agents can now analyze large volumes of software code to identify vulnerabilities (Wang
et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026). Bad actors can use them as powerful tools to discover and subsequently
exploit zero-day vulnerabilities in widely used software (Carlini et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a;
Lee & Brumley, 2026). Yet many companies and institutions lack the computational resources to
scan their own software using advanced agents, leaving them vulnerable to attackers wielding more
powerful ones. Less resource-rich stakeholders need a way to level the playing field, a way to slow
down attackers long enough to give themselves time to identify and repair their own software.
In our analysis of agent trajectories in CyberGym (Wang et al., 2026b), we make surprising observations that different versions of the same codebase often exhibit varying levels of resilience to AI
agents scanning for vulnerabilities (Section 2.2). More specifically, within a single repository, the
agent’s success rate in vulnerability analysis fluctuates significantly across adjacent code commits
that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability (Figure 1). In many cases, the agent either
fails to identify the vulnerability after exhausting the budget or generates false positives in which the
proof-of-concept (PoC) input cannot trigger the vulnerability. Such a pattern is consistently observed
across multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
This finding suggests that agents’ ability to identify software vulnerabilities is highly dependent on the
code representation (i.e., syntax and structure) used in real-world software development. It further
prompts us to consider the concept of natural and functionality-preserving code transformations,
and their potential as a defense to slow down or even stall attacker agents. Conceptually, natural,
functionality-preserving code transformations are like “imperceptible adversarial perturbations” in
the image domain (Szegedy et al., 2013), which are intentional content modifications that preserve the
original content’s primary utility while manipulating how it gets interpreted and used by AI models.

chk_data.paper_excerpt:
M INING AND A PPLYING NATURAL C ODE T RANSFORMATIONS

Having established the potential benefits of natural code transformations, we now explore how to
mine them from real-world development activities while keeping them broadly applicable to diverse
codebases. First, we mine recurring development patterns, e.g., refactoring activities, from code commits and organize them into base transformations represented as agent skills. We then use a coding
agent to localize applicable program points and implement these skills as concrete transformations.
We evaluate their efficacy as a potential defense against vulnerability analysis agents in Section 4.
Mining transformation categories from existing codebases We group recurring development
patterns into transformation categories, e.g., extracting duplicated cleanup code into a shared utility
function. The categories abstract away commit-specific names and locations so the same transformation can be applied to other repositories. Specifically, we use CommitPackFT (Muennighoff et al.,
2024), which contains 702,062 real-world commits across 14 major software development tasks (e.g.,
refactoring, cleanup, etc.) paired with instruction-like commit messages. Given that existing agentic
vulnerability analysis targets primarily memory-unsafe languages, we focus on C and C++ commits.
After removing duplicate commits and those with fewer than ten changed lines, we retain 1,196 C
commits and 851 C++ commits for mining base transformations.
We iteratively apply DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) to extract up to three atomic transformations per commit. Each action follows the form action + concrete code element + purpose, e.g.,
extract into a helper + duplicated cleanup statements + to centralize resource release. The transformation is described independently of the particular functions and variables modified by the commit.
4

S1

DATA S AMPLING S TATS

We selected our tasks from the popular CyberGym benchmark (Wang et al., 2026b), which contains 1,507 repo-level vulnerability detection tasks with ground-truth PoCs from 188 real-world
open-source projects, covering 28 crash types. We construct a smaller subset that still preserves
the distribution of the original benchmark and covers diverse characteristics. Since there are 188
source projects used in CyberGym, we made sure to get exactly one task from each project. However, there were 151 tasks with zero-byte PoCs or repeated crash-site reports. After excluding these,
we were left with 186 projects.
Representative subset. We wanted our subset to be representative of the CyberGym dataset, so
we focused on balancing the project source, codebase size (lines of code), the crash type, PoC size
(in bytes), crash stack depth, and the SCARINESS (sanitizer) score used in CyberGym’s original
sampling method (Wang et al., 2026b). This gave us 186 tasks from the 186 projects covering 26
crash types, and the numerical feature distributions are visualized in Figure 7. As a minor difference,
our subset reduces the share of heap-buffer-overflow tasks from 38.8% to 25.3% and increases the
share of UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer reports from 6.6% to 13.4%. Given that balance is useful in
this kind of sampling, and there were only three sanitizers used, this is a reasonable change.
